plan: Paired passages (CLD-P-ACT-R-000006) to raise Integration of Knowledge and Ideas share; cross-passage traps; R005-02 and R005-06 resubmitted.

passages.title: Street Trees (paired passages)
passages.text:
Passage A

On a July afternoon, the asphalt of an unshaded parking lot can grow far hotter than the air above it, while the pavement beneath a mature tree a few steps away stays markedly cooler. Multiply that difference across a neighborhood and the effect is measurable: blocks with dense tree canopy are often several degrees cooler than nearby blocks with little shade. For cities facing longer and more frequent heat waves, this makes street trees something more than decoration. They are infrastructure, as essential in their way as storm drains or power lines, and they deserve to be funded like it.

The comparison is not merely rhetorical. A tree, like a water main, delivers its benefits for decades, but only if it survives its vulnerable early years. Cities that count trees as infrastructure tend to budget not just for planting but for watering, pruning, and replacement—the unglamorous maintenance that turns a sapling into shade.

Passage B

Announcements of tree-planting campaigns are a fixture of city politics. A mayor promises a hundred thousand new trees; volunteers dig holes; photographs are taken. Five years later, a sizable share of those trees may be dead, killed by drought, road salt, or simple neglect. And the neighborhoods that most needed shade may have received the fewest saplings to begin with, because planting programs often depend on residents to request trees and to agree to water them.

None of this means planting is a mistake. But a count of trees planted measures effort, not results. The figure that matters is canopy—how much shade actually exists, and where. A city that plants fewer trees but keeps them alive, and that places them deliberately in the hottest, least-shaded blocks, may do more good than one that plants many and tracks none.

passages.title: Why Ice Is Slippery
passages.text:
Ask most people why ice is slippery and they will offer an explanation they probably learned in school: the weight of a skater presses on the ice, the pressure melts a thin film of water, and the blade glides on that film. The account is tidy, memorable, and, according to most physicists who have checked the numbers, largely wrong.

Pressure does lower the temperature at which ice melts, but only slightly. Even the narrow blade of a skate, concentrating a person's full weight on a sliver of steel, lowers the melting point by only a few degrees at most. That might matter on a mild afternoon, when the ice is already close to melting. It cannot explain why people slip on sidewalks at fifteen degrees below zero, or why a stationary shoe, pressing far less sharply than a blade, slides just as readily.

A second explanation shifts attention from pressure to motion. When an object slides across ice, friction generates heat, and that heat may melt a thin layer of water at the point of contact. Experiments have supported this idea for fast-moving objects such as skates and sled runners. But friction requires movement, and ice is slippery even at the very first instant of a step, before any appreciable heat could build up.

The explanation that has gained the most support in recent decades was first suggested in the 1850s by the physicist Michael Faraday. Faraday proposed that the surface of ice is never entirely solid. The molecules in the outermost layer, he reasoned, have fewer neighbors to hold them in place than molecules deeper inside, and so they remain loosely bound, behaving more like a liquid than a solid even well below the freezing point. Modern measurements have detected such a layer, though researchers still debate how thick it is, how liquid-like it really is, and how it changes with temperature.

None of this means that pressure and friction play no role. On a rink, all three effects may operate at once, and their relative importance likely shifts with temperature, speed, and the materials involved. What has changed is the order of the story. The surface of ice, it turns out, is slippery before anyone steps on it.

candidates.stem: The author of Passage A primarily argues that street trees:

choices.A: cool neighborhoods mainly by shading paved parking lots.
choices.B: are more effective than storm drains at lowering temperatures.
choices.C: should be funded and maintained as essential city infrastructure.
choices.D: are mainly decorative features that cities tend to overvalue.

candidates.evidence: They are infrastructure, as essential in their way as storm drains or power lines, and they deserve to be funded like it.
candidates.explanation: Passage A builds from the cooling evidence to its claim: trees are infrastructure and deserve infrastructure-style funding, including maintenance.

A.rationale: The parking lot is an opening example, not the main claim.

B.rationale: Passage A compares trees to storm drains in importance, not in cooling.

D.rationale: Passage A says trees are "something more than decoration."

hints: Find the sentence that states what cities should do.

strategy.explanation: State Passage A's claim in one sentence, then match.

candidates.remember: The main claim is usually what the author says should happen.

candidates.stem: In Passage A, the comparison of a tree to a water main mainly serves to:

choices.A: stress that both provide long-term benefits only if they are cared for early on.
choices.B: argue that trees and water mains should be paid for from a single budget.
choices.C: suggest that tree roots often damage the pipes buried beneath city streets.
choices.D: show that water mains cost cities far more than street trees do over time.

candidates.evidence: delivers its benefits for decades, but only if it survives its vulnerable early years
candidates.explanation: Both deliver benefits for decades but only if they survive the early years, which supports the call for maintenance budgets.

B.rationale: Passage A compares how they deliver benefits, not how they are budgeted together.

hints: What do a tree and a water main have in common, according to the passage?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence containing the comparison and the one after it.

candidates.remember: Ask what point a comparison is used to make.

candidates.stem: According to Passage B, one reason the neighborhoods most in need of shade may receive fewer trees is that planting programs often:

choices.A: lose many young trees to road salt in those neighborhoods.
choices.B: favor places where mayors can be photographed with volunteers.
choices.C: lack enough open space in those neighborhoods to plant trees.
choices.D: rely on residents to request trees and to agree to water them.

candidates.evidence: because planting programs often depend on residents to request trees and to agree to water them
candidates.explanation: Passage B says the neediest neighborhoods may get the fewest saplings "because planting programs often depend on residents to request trees and to agree to water them."

A.rationale: Road salt is listed as a cause of tree death, not of uneven distribution.

B.rationale: Photographs are mentioned, but not as the reason for uneven distribution.

hints: Find the word "because" in the first paragraph of Passage B.
candidates.remember: Detail questions are answered by a specific sentence.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in Passage B, the word "fixture" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: Announcements of tree-planting campaigns are a fixture of city politics.
candidates.explanation: The examples that follow (a mayor's promise, volunteers, photographs) describe something that happens routinely, so "fixture" means a regular feature.

A.rationale: This is the household meaning (a light fixture), which does not fit announcements.

C.rationale: This is the sports meaning, which does not fit.

hints: Substitute each choice into the sentence.

strategy.explanation: Replace the word with your own: "common part."

candidates.remember: Test meanings in the sentence, not from memory.

candidates.stem: The author of Passage B would most likely regard a city's announcement that it planted 50,000 trees last year as:

choices.A: proof that the city's planting program has largely failed.
choices.B: evidence that the neediest neighborhoods were well served.
choices.C: insufficient evidence by itself that the city's shade has increased.
choices.D: a meaningless figure that cities should stop reporting.

candidates.evidence: But a count of trees planted measures effort, not results.
candidates.explanation: Passage B says a count of trees planted measures effort, not results; what matters is surviving canopy and where it is. So the announcement alone does not show more shade.

A.rationale: Passage B says planting is not a mistake; a count shows effort, not failure.

B.rationale: A total count says nothing about where trees went.

D.rationale: The author says the count "measures effort," so it is not meaningless.

hints: What does Passage B say a count of trees measures?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that are more extreme than the author.

candidates.remember: Match the author's degree of certainty.

candidates.stem: Both authors would most likely agree that:

choices.A: cities should plant as many trees as they can, as quickly as they can.
choices.B: tree canopy has little measurable effect on neighborhood temperatures.
choices.C: nearby residents should be responsible for watering new street trees.
choices.D: a tree-planting program's success depends heavily on care after planting.

candidates.evidence: the unglamorous maintenance that turns a sapling into shade
candidates.explanation: Passage A calls for budgets for watering, pruning and replacement; Passage B values a city that "keeps them alive." Both stress care after planting.

A.rationale: Passage B argues that fewer, well-tended trees may do more good.

B.rationale: Passage A says canopy makes blocks several degrees cooler.

C.rationale: Passage B criticizes programs that depend on residents.

hints: What does each passage say about what happens after planting?

strategy.explanation: Find one supporting line in each passage.

candidates.remember: An agreement answer needs support in both passages.

candidates.subskill: How one author would respond to the other
candidates.stem: How would the author of Passage B most likely respond to Passage A's claim that trees deserve to be "funded like" infrastructure?

choices.A: By rejecting it, on the grounds that planting campaigns are mostly political theater.
choices.B: By agreeing, while insisting that such funding be judged by surviving shade where it is most needed.
choices.C: By arguing that street trees cool neighborhoods much less than Passage A suggests.
choices.D: By proposing that storm drains and power lines should be funded ahead of trees.

candidates.evidence: The figure that matters is canopy—how much shade actually exists, and where.
candidates.explanation: Passage B mocks planting announcements but does not reject planting; its standard is canopy that survives and is placed in the hottest blocks. It would welcome serious funding as long as success is measured that way.

A.rationale: Passage B says "None of this means planting is a mistake."

C.rationale: Passage B never disputes the cooling effect.

D.rationale: Passage B does not discuss other infrastructure.

hints: What does Passage B say should be measured?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate responses Passage B's text contradicts.

candidates.remember: Criticism of how something is done is not rejection of doing it.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes a difference in focus between the two passages?

choices.A: Passage A explains why trees are valuable; Passage B examines how planting efforts are judged and distributed.
choices.B: Passage A criticizes city politicians; Passage B praises the volunteers who plant trees.
choices.C: Passage A relies chiefly on statistics; Passage B relies chiefly on personal anecdotes.
choices.D: Passage A focuses on young saplings; Passage B focuses on old, mature trees.

candidates.evidence: But a count of trees planted measures effort, not results.
candidates.explanation: Passage A makes the case for trees' value as infrastructure; Passage B shifts to how programs are measured (count versus canopy) and where trees go.

B.rationale: Passage A does not criticize politicians, and Passage B does not praise volunteers.

C.rationale: Neither passage relies on personal anecdotes, and Passage A uses few statistics.

D.rationale: Passage B discusses newly planted trees dying; Passage A discusses mature trees' shade.

hints: Summarize each passage in a phrase.

strategy.explanation: Summarize both passages before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Both halves of a comparison choice must be accurate.

candidates.stem: According to Passage A, cities that treat trees as infrastructure tend to:

choices.A: plant fewer trees than other cities do.
choices.B: require residents to water the new trees.
choices.C: count trees planted to measure success.
choices.D: budget for maintenance as well as for planting.

candidates.evidence: budget not just for planting but for watering, pruning, and replacement
candidates.explanation: Passage A says such cities "budget not just for planting but for watering, pruning, and replacement."

A.rationale: This echoes Passage B's suggestion, not Passage A.

B.rationale: Passage B, not Passage A, discusses relying on residents.

C.rationale: Passage A never mentions this; Passage B criticizes it.

hints: Make sure you are reading Passage A, not Passage B.

strategy.explanation: Find the sentence beginning "Cities that count trees."

candidates.remember: With paired passages, check which passage the question asks about.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, which observation can the pressure explanation NOT account for?

choices.A: A shoe that is not moving slides as readily as a skate blade does.
choices.B: Skates glide more easily on ice that is already close to melting.
choices.C: A narrow skate blade presses harder on ice than a broad boot does.
choices.D: The melting point of ice drops slightly as pressure on it increases.

candidates.evidence: or why a stationary shoe, pressing far less sharply than a blade, slides just as readily
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists two things the pressure explanation cannot explain: slipping at fifteen degrees below zero and a stationary shoe sliding as readily as a blade.

B.rationale: The passage says pressure "might matter" in that case, so the explanation can account for it.

C.rationale: This is consistent with the pressure explanation; it is not something the explanation fails to account for.

D.rationale: This is the fact the pressure explanation is built on.

hints: Find the sentence beginning "It cannot explain."

strategy.explanation: Locate the paragraph that tests the pressure explanation.

candidates.remember: Watch for NOT in the stem.
candidates.revision_note: R005-02 resubmitted: a blind solver noted that the old choice C (friction heating under sled runners) is also unexplained by pressure on a literal reading; C now states something the pressure explanation is consistent with.

candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Faraday's explanation over the friction explanation?

choices.A: A skate blade slides faster as it warms the ice directly beneath it.
choices.B: An object resting on ice begins sliding easily before any measurable heating occurs.
choices.C: Ice becomes more slippery as the weight pressing on it increases.
choices.D: Ice that forms from seawater melts at a lower temperature than freshwater ice.

candidates.evidence: and so they remain loosely bound, behaving more like a liquid than a solid even well below the freezing point
candidates.explanation: Friction requires motion and heat; Faraday's layer exists before any motion. Easy sliding before any heating fits Faraday and contradicts what friction would require.

A.rationale: Heating that increases sliding supports the friction explanation.

C.rationale: This bears on the pressure explanation, not on Faraday versus friction.

D.rationale: Salt content affects melting point but says nothing about whether surface layers or friction cause slipperiness.

hints: What does friction need that Faraday's layer does not?

strategy.explanation: For each finding, ask which explanation it favors.

candidates.remember: To favor one explanation, find what only it predicts.
candidates.revision_note: R005-06 resubmitted: relabelled medium (blind solvers rated it easy/medium), and the altitude distractor, which stated a scientifically backwards claim, replaced with an accurate but irrelevant fact.
